chunks: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I am a man who is a muezzin. So whenever it was a cloudy day, I could not recognize the time.'
So he said: 'When the rooster crows three consecutive times, the sun has declined and the time for salat has entered.'

key_terms.زَالَتِ الشَّمْسُ: The sun has declined (zawal) — the moment the sun passes its zenith, marking the beginning of Dhuhr prayer time
key_terms.مُؤَذِّنٌ: Muezzin — the person who calls the adhan (call to prayer), responsible for announcing prayer times
key_terms.وَقْتُ الصَّلَاةِ: Time of salat — the prescribed prayer time, here specifically Dhuhr (noon prayer)
key_terms.وِلَاءً: Consecutively — one after another without interruption
key_terms.يَوْمُ الْغَيْمِ: Cloudy day — a day when overcast skies prevent visual determination of the sun's position

ai.seo_question: How did Imam al-Sadiq say to determine prayer time on a cloudy day?
ai.summary: A muezzin (caller to prayer) asks Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) how to determine the time for the noon prayer (Dhuhr) on cloudy days when the sun's position is obscured. The Imam provides a practical natural sign: three consecutive crows of a rooster indicate that the sun has passed its zenith and the time for salat has entered. This hadith reflects the early Islamic community's reliance on observable natural signs when astronomical observation was impossible, and demonstrates the Imam's role as a practical jurisprudential guide for the community.
